notes:
I have gathered substantial material from several key commentaries. Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

---

## Psalm 97 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Overview

The psalm is a theophany — a poetic depiction of God appearing in awesome majesty as King and Judge. Spurgeon divides it into four strophes of three verses each: the coming of the Lord (vv. 1–3), its effect on the earth (vv. 4–6), its effect on the heathen and God’s people (vv. 7–9), and exhortation with encouragement for the righteous (vv. 10–12).
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Matthew Henry says Christ is the Alpha and Omega of this psalm: “He it is that reigns, to the joy of all mankind”; His government speaks terror to enemies (vv. 2–7) and comfort to His friends (vv. 8–12).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/97.htm

Gill, the Baptist expositor, says the psalm “respects the kingdom of Christ, from his first to his second coming.” The Syriac version calls it “a Psalm of David, in which he prophesies concerning the coming of the Messiah, and again he intimates in it his last appearance.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-97.html

---

### v. 1 — “The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the distant shores be glad.”

**Traditional reading:** The psalm opens with the great declaration “Jehovah reigns.” Adam Clarke (quoted by Guzik) calls this “a self-evident axiom” — God is infinite, eternal, all-powerful, and must be Governor of all things. The reign of Yahweh is active, not passive; God is not a “watchmaker” who retreats from His creation.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-97/

Ellicott notes that “the multitude of isles” reflects a wide gaze to the west, embracing the coasts and islands of the Mediterranean (and possibly beyond), which he marks as characteristic of post-exilic literature.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/97.htm

The Pulpit Commentary says “the isles” represent “the abode of the Gentiles” — they too will be benefited by God’s coming reign.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/97.htm

Spurgeon adds that the phrase “let the multitude of isles be glad” is equivalent to “all lands reached by ships.” He notes that “upon actual islands some of the greatest victories of the Cross have been achieved,” citing Britain and the islands of Polynesia.
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Matthew Henry similarly applies this to the Gentiles, whose countries are called “the isles of the Gentiles” (Genesis 10:5): “There is enough in Christ for the multitude of the isles to rejoice in; for, though many have been made happy in him, yet still there is room.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/97.htm

---

### v. 2 — “Clouds and darkness surround Him; righteousness and justice are His throne’s foundation.”

**Traditional reading:** The imagery is drawn from the theophany at Sinai (Exodus 19:9, 16; 20:21). Guzik, citing Kidner, says: “Clouds and thick darkness warn of his unapproachable holiness and hiddenness to presumptuous man,” while the fire and lightning in the following verses “reveal a holiness that is also devouring and irresistible (cf. Heb. 12:29).”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-97/

Ellicott calls the pairing of “clouds and darkness” with “righteousness and judgment” a mark of a “truly poetic mind.” The immediate effect on the Hebrew mind was not fear but “a sublime sense of safety in the established right and truth of God.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/97.htm

The Pulpit Commentary observes that the darkness “does not belong to the nature of God, who ‘is Light, and in him is no darkness at all’ (1 John 1:5), but to the interrelationship between God and man, in which are involved problems that man cannot solve.”
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/97.htm

Spurgeon makes the theological point that “Jehovah is an autocrat, but not a despot. Absolute power is safe in the hands of him who cannot err, or act unrighteously.” The clouds also teach “the impertinence of attempting to pry into the essence of the Godhead.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Gill sees the clouds and darkness as pointing to “the obscurity of his divine nature at his first coming” — Christ appearing in the form of a servant, so that few discerned His glory — and also to the dark providences that attended the first setting up of His kingdom.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-97.html

**Denominational note — Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin resists “refined renderings” that spiritualise the clouds too far. He argues the psalmist intended the darkness simply to impress hearts with reverential fear of God: “A cloudy sky overawes us more than a clear one, as the darkness produces a peculiar effect upon the senses.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-97.html (excerpt in search results)

---

### v. 3 — “Fire goes before Him and consumes His foes on every side.”

**Traditional reading:** Again, Sinai imagery dominates (Exodus 19:16–20). The fire is an “advance guard clearing the way.” Guzik says this is a poetic description either of what God did at Sinai or of a future display of His sovereign presence.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-97/

Ellicott notes this is an echo of Psalm 50:3 (also Psalm 18:8; Habakkuk 3:4–5).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/97.htm

The Pulpit Commentary: “So long as there is evil in the world, the ‘fire’ of God’s wrath must necessarily ‘go before him’ at each theophany, to sweep the evil from his path … in this sense ‘our God is a consuming fire’ (Hebrews 12:29).”
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/97.htm

Spurgeon, reading the verse through a New Testament lens, says: “Even now where the gospel is preached in faith, and in the power of the Spirit, it burns its own way, irresistibly destroying falsehood, superstition, unbelief, sin, indifference, and hardness of heart.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Gill, likewise, interprets the fire as the Gospel: “as it enlightens, warms, comforts, and refreshes his people, [it] searches, torments, and destroys his enemies.” He also sees a fulfilment in the Roman destruction of Jerusalem (Matthew 22:7) and in the final judgment.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-97.html

---

### v. 4 — “His lightning illuminates the world; the earth sees and trembles.”

**Traditional reading:** The Pulpit Commentary notes the tenses switch from present to past here — “not that any past event is alluded to, but merely to mark prophetic certainty. The psalmist, rapt in vision, sees the future as past.”
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/97.htm

Ellicott says this verse is taken from Psalm 77:17–18.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/97.htm

Spurgeon applies it to the apostolic age: “Jesus in the gospel lights up the earth with such a blaze of truth and grace as was never seen or even imagined before… nothing ever caused such a shaking and commotion as the proclamation of the gospel, it turned the world upside down.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Gill interprets the lightning as the swift progress of Gospel doctrine: “by the apostles they were published in all nations, and were the means of enlightening them in the true knowledge of themselves, and of the way of salvation by Christ.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-97.html

---

### v. 5 — “The mountains melt like wax at the presence of the LORD, before the Lord of all the earth.”

**Traditional reading:** The Pulpit Commentary: the earth itself is regarded “as not only shaken (v. 4), but as melting and crumbling away at the descent of God from heaven to earth (comp. 2 Peter 3:10).”
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/97.htm

Spurgeon: “Men cannot move the hills, with difficulty do they climb them, with incredible toil do they pierce their way through their fastnesses, but it is not so with the Lord, his presence makes a clear pathway, obstacles disappear, a highway is made, and that not by his hand as though it cost him pains, but by his mere presence, for power goes forth from him with a word or a glance.” He also applies it to “states and kingdoms which stand out upon the world like mountains” that are “utterly dissolved when he decrees their end.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Gill says that at Christ’s coming “every mountain and island were moved out of their places” (Revelation 6:14), and that the proud and lofty “shall melt at his presence.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-97.html

Ellicott notes that “the Lord of the whole earth” is a title first found in Joshua 3:11, 13, emphasising God’s triumph over heathen gods in leading Israel into Canaan.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/97.htm

Guzik, citing Maclaren, notes the parallelism of “LORD” (YHWH) and “Lord” (Adonai) in this verse affirms that “Yahweh is the Lord (‘great King’) of all the earth.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-97/

---

### v. 6 — “The heavens proclaim His righteousness; all the peoples see His glory.”

**Traditional reading:** The Pulpit Commentary says the heavens proclaim this “by signs in the heavens … that the Lord has come to judgment. And all the people see (rather, have seen) his glory; literally, all the peoples; i.e. all the nations of the earth.”
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/97.htm

Ellicott: “At length the world at large is convinced, by visible manifestations, of what Israel had recognised through the veil of darkness and cloud — the eternal righteousness of which all the splendours of the storm have been a witness.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/97.htm

Spurgeon says it is “not mere poetry, for a great truth underlies it, the whole creation has been made to groan through man’s sin, and it is yet to share in the joy of his restoration.” He sees the Gospel as becoming “so well known and widely promulgated, that it seemed to be proclaimed by every star.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Gill sees the “heavens” as possibly referring to the angels (as the Targum renders it) or to Gospel ministers (“men of heavenly gifts and grace”) who “declare the justifying righteousness of Christ.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-97.html

---

### v. 7 — “All worshipers of images are put to shame — those who boast in idols. Worship Him, all you gods!”

**Traditional reading:** Ellicott explains that “idols” in Hebrew means “empty, worthless things, shaming those who worship them.” He notes it is doubtful whether the verbs are imperatives or statements of fact; the LXX and Vulgate take them as imperatives.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/97.htm

The Pulpit Commentary: “The display of real Divine power makes manifest the impotency of the idols, and puts their worshippers to the blush. … The theophany is a call on the false gods to worship the true God.”
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/97.htm

**A key New Testament connection:** The phrase “Worship Him, all you gods!” is quoted in Hebrews 1:6 (from the LXX of Deuteronomy 32:43) as referring to the angels worshipping Christ at His incarnation. Gill builds a full argument from this: it proves “Christ is superior to angels,” “that he is truly God, since God only is the object of religious worship,” “that if he is worshipped by angels, he ought to be worshipped by men,” and “that angels are not the proper objects of worship, since they are worshippers.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-97.html

Spurgeon, with characteristic vividness, writes: “Let Jove do homage to Jehovah, let Thor lay down his hammer at the foot of the cross, and Juggernaut remove his blood stained car out of the road of Immanuel.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Ellicott clarifies that “all ye gods” does not mean “angels” (as in the LXX rendering of Psalm 8:5), but here “the term is directly intended to include among superhuman beings the agencies worshipped by heathen nations as deities.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/97.htm

---

### v. 8 — “Zion hears and rejoices, and the towns of Judah exult because of Your judgments, O LORD.”

**Traditional reading:** Ellicott says this echoes Psalm 48:11.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/97.htm

The Pulpit Commentary: “To Zion, the Church of God, the company of his saints, the theophany brings, not shame, but rejoicing. The Lord comes for their relief, for their deliverance, for their exaltation.” It adds that the “daughters of Judah” are “the other cities of Judaea besides Jerusalem,” and in a Christian sense “the irregularly organized Churches, which will participate in the general joy of the faithful at Christ’s final coming.”
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/97.htm

Spurgeon applies it to the first Christian centuries: “In the first ages of Christianity the believing Israel rejoiced to see Christ’s kingdom victorious among the heathen.” He also believes in a future fulfilment: “The day shall come when the literal Zion, so long forsaken, shall joy in the common salvation.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Gill interprets “Zion” as the church of Christ (Hebrews 12:22) and “the daughters of Judah” as “particular congregated churches, particular believers and professors of Christ.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-97.html

Matthew Henry notes that the faithful rejoice “because God is glorified, and whatever redounds to his honour is very much his people’s pleasure.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/97.htm

---

### v. 9 — “For You, O LORD, are Most High over all the earth; You are exalted far above all gods.”

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist shifts from speaking about God to addressing God directly. The Pulpit Commentary: “No comparison can be made between Jehovah and the heathen gods. He is ‘exalted’ far, far above them.”
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/97.htm

Spurgeon: “As much as ALL is exalted above nothing, and perfection above folly. … The days are on their way when all men shall discern this truth, and shall render unto the Lord the glory which is due alone to him.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Gill notes the use of “Elion” (Most High), indicating Christ’s dignity as a divine Person. He says Christ is “exalted far above all gods” — not only false deities and earthly rulers, “but also than the angels in heaven; he is set down at the right hand of God, where they are not, and never were, nor shall be.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-97.html

Guzik notes John Trapp connected this verse with Ephesians 1:21: Christ is “far above all principality and power and might and dominion.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-97/

---

### v. 10 — “Hate evil, O you who love the LORD! He preserves the souls of His saints; He delivers them from the hand of the wicked.”

**Traditional reading:** Guzik says this is one of the most often broken commands among God’s people: “We find it easy to be too loving, or rather express a twisted love that pretends to both love the LORD and love or accept the things that He hates.” He adds that we may be angry at sin’s consequences without truly hating it enough to repent and forsake it.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-97/

Ellicott prefers to point the Hebrew as an indicative rather than imperative: “They who love Jehovah, hate evil,” to avoid what he sees as an “awkward transition” to the next clause. He adds: “Love of God implies the hatred of all He hates.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/97.htm

The Pulpit Commentary: “It is indifference to evil, that, more than anything else, lays men open to the assaults of Satan.”
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/97.htm

Spurgeon: “We cannot love God without hating that which he hates. We are not only to avoid evil, and to refuse to countenance it, but we must be in arms against it, and bear towards it a hearty indignation.” On God’s preservation, he notes: “He may leave the bodies of his persecuted saints in the hand of the wicked, but not their souls, these are very dear to him, and he preserves them safe in his bosom.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Gill says “he preserveth the souls of his saints” means preserving them “from the evil of sin, from its governing and damning power, from a final and total apostasy by it, from ruin and destruction through it.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-97.html

Matthew Henry: “It is the immortal soul that Christ preserves, the inward man, which may be renewed more and more when the outward man decays. He will preserve the souls of his saints from sin, from apostasy, and despair, under their greatest trials.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/97.htm

**Denominational note — Baptist (perseverance of the saints):** Gill’s language about preservation from “final and total apostasy” reflects the Baptist/Reformed doctrine of the perseverance of the saints. This is a point where Baptist and Reformed traditions largely agree, in contrast to traditions (such as classical Arminian/Wesleyan) that hold believers can fall from grace.

---

### v. 11 — “Light shines on the righteous, gladness on the upright in heart.” (BSB)

*(Note: The BSB renders this as “Light shines” rather than “Light is sown.”)*

**Traditional reading:** Most older English versions translate the Hebrew as “Light is sown for the righteous” (e.g., KJV). The Pulpit Commentary says God “sheds the rays of his grace on the path of the righteous man, enlightens his understanding, and illumines his spirit perpetually.” Together with light, He sheds abroad “gladness, the irrepressible joy which comes from a sense of his favour and protection.”
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/97.htm

Ellicott says the metaphor of “sowing” light “must not be pressed so as to think of a harvest to come. The image is an obvious and common one.” He cites Lucretius and Milton as using similar imagery.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/97.htm

Spurgeon: “All along their pathway it is strewn. Their night is almost over, their day is coming … The full harvest of delight is not yet ours, but it is sown for us; it is springing, it will yet appear in fulness.” He adds: “God has lightning for sinners and light for saints.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Guzik, citing F.B. Meyer: “You do not realize it, but you are sowing light. Each act of self-denial, in which you cast yourself into the ground to die, is a seed-germ of the harvest of gladness.” And citing Adam Clarke: “Every grace of God is a seed, which he intends should produce a thousand fold in the hearts of genuine believers. … Let the light and gladness be faithfully cultivated, and they will multiply themselves till the whole body shall be full of light, and the whole soul full of happiness.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-97/

**Text-critical note:** Guzik notes that Derek Kidner argues “Light dawns” is “surely the right reading here, following one Hebrew manuscript and all the ancient versions.” The BSB (“Light shines”) follows this alternative reading. Gill reports that “the Septuagint, Vulgate Latin, and all the Oriental versions, render it, ‘light is risen for the righteous.’”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-97/ and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-97.html

---

### v. 12 — “Rejoice in the LORD, you righteous ones, and praise His holy name.”

**Traditional reading:** The psalm ends as it began — with a call to rejoice. The Pulpit Commentary: the righteous are “finally exhorted to ‘rejoice in the Lord,’ i.e. to show forth their gratitude to God in psalms and hymns of joy,” and to “give thanks to his holy memorial, which is the same as giving thanks to his Name.”
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/97.htm

Matthew Henry: “Let all the streams of comfort, which flow to us in the channel of Christ’s kingdom, lead us to the fountain, and oblige us to rejoice in the Lord. All the lines of joy must meet in him as in the centre.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/97.htm

Guzik: “The rejoicing should not be primarily in what He has given, but in the LORD Himself.” James Montgomery Boice is cited: “It began by calling upon the people of the whole earth to rejoice in God’s rule (Psalm 97:1). It ends by calling upon us to lead the way in this worship.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-97/

Spurgeon: “‘Give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness’ — which is the harmony of all his attributes, the superlative wholeness of his character. This is a terror to the wicked, and a cause of thankfulness to the gracious. … The holiness of the religion of Jesus is its glory, it is that which makes it glad tidings, since while man is left in his sins no bliss can be his portion.”
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php

Matthew Henry adds an important distinction: “Sinners tremble, but saints rejoice, at the remembrance of God’s holiness.” He notes that those who hate sin themselves “are glad that God does so, in hopes that therefore he will not suffer it to have dominion over them.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/97.htm

---

## Summary of Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**1. The “Light is sown” vs. “Light dawns” question (v. 11):** The older Protestant tradition (KJV, and with it Spurgeon, Gill, Matthew Henry, the Pulpit Commentary) reads “light is sown,” drawing out a metaphor of seed, growth, and future harvest. Modern translations and some commentators (Kidner, and the BSB) prefer “light dawns” or “light shines,” following ancient versions and a Hebrew manuscript. This is a textual rather than strictly doctrinal difference, but it affects application: the “sown” reading emphasizes patient waiting for a future harvest of joy; the “shines/dawns” reading emphasizes present possession of light.

**2. Perseverance of the saints (v. 10):** Gill (Baptist) and Spurgeon (Baptist) speak of God preserving the saints from “final and total apostasy.” Calvin, in his excerpted notes, also emphasises God’s preserving work. A Wesleyan/Arminian reading (not found in my searches) would typically emphasise the human responsibility to “hate evil” as a condition of continued preservation, while still affirming God’s keeping power.

**3. Authorship and dating:** Spurgeon strongly defends Davidic authorship against “modern critics” who date the psalm post-exile. Lange’s Commentary notes that the psalm’s language and affinities with Second Isaiah suggest a post-exilic setting (possibly after the fall of Babylon), while also acknowledging that it is “eminently suited to represent typically … epoch-making” theophanic events in salvation history.
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps097.php and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/psalms-97.html

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

Lange’s Commentary (a more critical work) notes: “The use of the præterite in the second and third strophes must not be disregarded,” and cites Perowne who says the past tenses “are most naturally explained as occasioned by some historical event, some great national deliverance or triumph of recent occurrence, such, for instance, as the overthrow of Babylon and the restoration of the Theocracy.” However, Lange himself leans toward a prophetic rather than purely historical reading, connecting the psalm to “the coming of the great and terrible day of the Lord.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/psalms-97.html

Hupfeld (cited by Lange) regards the psalm as having no historical occasion at all, but as “a free, poetical working up of current images and forms of expression” — the extreme opposite of the Messianic view.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/psalms-97.html

*(Note: I was unable to search bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org for additional modern scholarship due to search limits being reached.)*

### Catholic and Orthodox

No Catholic or Orthodox sources (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) were retrieved within the search limits. If these are desired, a further round of searching would be needed.

### Debated Popular Modern Teaching

No results were retrieved regarding prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace readings of this psalm. The psalm’s subject matter (God’s majestic reign, judgment on enemies, call to hate evil) does not lend itself naturally to those interpretive frameworks, which may explain the absence of such readings in the search results.
